title: 20 steam turbines to combine for 1 GW of power for data centers
content: Babcock & Wilcox, a longtime power-generation technology provider, is set to work on 20 steam turbine generator sets with a combined capacity of 1 gigawatt, targeting projects that need large amounts of power on accelerated timelines.The agreement with Siemens Energy covers 20 turbine sets rated at 50 megawatts each. B&W plans to deploy them through its FastPower program, which focuses on supplying power-generation equipment for data center and other large-scale power projects.The deal comes as electricity demand from data centers continues to rise. Large computing facilities need steady power around the clock, creating pressure to bring new generation capacity online faster.Steam turbines are a mature technology for large-scale electricity generation. In a typical system, steam produced by heating water drives turbine blades, which turn a generator to produce electricity. Their established use in power plants makes them suitable for projects seeking dependable generation at substantial scale.One gigawatt moves fasterB&W said the agreement strengthens its ability to respond to customers looking for power without lengthy project schedules. The company said it has a pipeline of near-term opportunities involving data centers and power generation.“As demand for dependable, large-scale power generation continues to accelerate, particularly from AI data center customers, we are strengthening our collaboration with Siemens Energy through this agreement,” said Brandy Johnson, Chief Technology Officer, B&W.“This order secures 1 GW of capacity and further positions us to deliver reliable, high-capacity energy solutions on the accelerated timelines our customers require.”The 20 turbine sets represent enough combined generating capacity to power a large electricity load, although the actual output available to individual customers will depend on how the systems are configured and deployed.B&W’s FastPower program is aimed at shortening the path from equipment procurement to operational power generation. That approach is becoming increasingly important as data center developers compete for access to electricity and grid connections.Turbines target hungry gridsThe partnership also gives Siemens Energy another route into the growing US market for large-scale power infrastructure. The company will provide its steam turbine technology for the generator sets covered by the agreement.“Siemens Energy’s agreement with Babcock & Wilcox to commence work on these steam turbine generator sets reflects a broader trend we are currently seeing in the U.S. market: growing demand for reliable, affordable, and resilient energy infrastructure,” said Tobias Panse, Senior Vice President of Steam Turbines and Generators for Siemens Energy.B&W said its experience with thousands of power-generation installations worldwide provides a foundation for delivering the equipment. The company is targeting not only data centers but also other large electricity projects where dependable generation is needed.The announcement does not identify the specific data center projects that will receive the turbine sets or provide individual delivery dates. It instead establishes the equipment capacity that B&W expects to support through its FastPower program.For Siemens Energy, the agreement adds to its work supplying turbine technology as utilities, industrial operators and data center developers look for additional generation. For B&W, the 1 GW commitment provides a significant equipment base for its effort to deliver power projects on shorter schedules.

title: 24-hour warning for ballistic missile tests: US, allies raise demand
content: Just a month after China shocked every nation with a long-range ballistic missile test in the Pacific, the U.S. and other countries have called for a warning before any such planned launch.The U.S. Department of State issued the ‘Joint Statement on Notifications of Ballistic Missile Launches’, which has also been signed by 40 other countries. The countries include Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Turkiye, Great Britain, among others.The call for issuing advance notifications includes prior notice for the launch of intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs), and space launch vehicles (SLVs) to affected states.The joint statement mentions that the recent missile testing in the Pacific region “did not follow the standard practices adopted by most states to notify and deconflict ICBM, SLBM, and SLV launches.” However, China is not named in the joint statement, but all references to the missile test point towards Beijing’s recent launch.Conducting nuclear-capable ballistic missile tests with advance noticeThe joint statement calls on all countries, particularly the ones which have nuclear weapons in their arsenal, to issue advance warning for ballistic missile launches. It goes on to add that conducting “nuclear-capable ballistic missile tests without sufficient advance notice and detail is dangerous and disrupts the peace and security of relevant nations in proximity to these tests.”Moreover, the joint statement warns that such tests increase the risk of miscalculation and undermine global stability and security. Further, it is incompatible with the responsibilities that come with possessing long-range missile capabilities.“We call on all countries, particularly nuclear-weapon States, that launch ICBMs, SLBMs, and SLVs to provide notification of such launches no less than 24 hours in advance,” the joint statement reads.It goes on to add that the advance notice should include other relevant information such as the generic class of the ballistic missile, the window for launch, area, and the direction. In addition, the countries conducting such a test should also include clear notes for airmen and mariners to reduce risk.“One hundred and forty-five countries participate in one such mechanism, the Hague Code of Conduct Against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (HCOC),” the joint statement reads. The U.S., Australia, South Korea, New Zealand, and others are signatories to the HCOC mechanism.The 41 countries stated that they are not against any form of weapon testing, military development, or operational needs. The joint statement aims to build confidence and reflect a shared commitment to security.China’s testing in JulyIn July 2026, China test-launched a ballistic missile in the Pacific Ocean. This was the first publicly known ballistic missile launch conducted by Beijing from a nuclear-powered submarine since 1982.The test was conducted on the day China and Russia were scheduled to begin their annual joint naval exercise. The exercise was going to be held near Qingdao, a military port on China’s east coast.Some countries in the region, including Japan and Australia among others, confirmed that they had been notified about the launch in advance. However, Australia had raised concerns that this long-range missile test could raise tensions in the Pacific.

title: 7 Biggest Sea Creatures Ever Discovered
content: The ocean is home to animals so enormous that some can outweigh entire groups of elephants, while others stretch farther than a city block. But deciding which one is the largest sea creature is not as simple as arranging them from biggest to smallest.Should size be measured by weight, length, or the dimensions of a single body—and should colonies count as one animal? To resolve that problem, this list focuses only on creatures alive today and gives each one a different, scientifically defensible record.1. Blue whale Wikimedia CommonsThe blue whale is the heaviest animal known to have lived, reaching around 30 meters (98 feet) and, in exceptional cases, an estimated 190 tonnes (209 US tons). Antarctic blue whales can also grow to approximately 33.5 meters (110 feet), although verified measurements vary between individuals. Despite their extraordinary bulk, blue whales survive primarily on krill. Their immense mouths expand during feeding, allowing them to engulf water and strain the tiny crustaceans through baleen plates. Their size surpasses every known dinosaur, making the biggest sea creature in the world also the largest animal in Earth’s history.2. Giant siphonophoreA giant siphonophore recorded off Western Australia in 2020 was estimated to measure approximately 45 meters (148 feet), making it possibly the longest marine animal colony directly observed. Researchers encountered it while exploring the Cape Range Canyon using a remotely operated vehicle. However, a siphonophore is not one animal in the conventional sense. It is a colony formed from numerous specialized units called zooids. Each performs a particular function, such as feeding, movement or reproduction, but cannot survive independently. That unusual biology complicates its claim to being the longest animal in the world.3. Lion’s mane jellyfish Wikimedia CommonsThe largest reported lion’s mane jellyfish stretched approximately 36.5 meters (120 feet) from the top of its bell to the ends of its tentacles. Its bell reportedly measured more than 2 meters (6.6 feet) across. That measurement should be treated cautiously because it comes from a poorly documented historical account. Smithsonian notes that more representative large specimens have bells approaching 1.8 meters (5.9 feet) and tentacles exceeding 15 meters (49 feet). The jellyfish uses its long, toxin-bearing tentacles to capture fish, plankton and other jellyfish in cold northern waters.4. Whale sharkWikimedia CommonsThe whale shark is the world’s largest living fish and can reportedly reach approximately 18 meters. However, most mature individuals are considerably smaller than that exceptional upper estimate.Despite being a shark, it is a filter-feeder rather than an active hunter of large prey. It swims with its mouth open, collecting plankton, fish eggs, and small marine animals. Its spotted skin pattern is unique to each individual, allowing researchers to identify and monitor particular sharks.5. Colossal squid The colossal squid is estimated to grow up to 7 meters (23 feet) long and weigh as much as 500 kilograms, making it the heaviest known invertebrate. Remarkably, scientists did not obtain confirmed footage of one alive in its natural habitat until March 9, 2025. The animal filmed near the South Sandwich Islands was a 30-centimeter (12-inch) juvenile swimming at a depth of 600 meters (1,969 feet).The sighting occurred exactly 100 years after the species was formally named. Before then, scientists mainly studied specimens caught accidentally or remains discovered inside whales, seabirds and fish.6. Sperm whale Male sperm whales can reach approximately 15.8 meters (52 feet) and weigh around 45 tonnes (50 US tons), making the species the largest toothed animal alive. They also possess the largest brain of any living animal.Unlike the filter-feeding blue whale, the sperm whale is an active deep-sea hunter. It uses powerful echolocation clicks to locate squid and fish in dark water, sometimes diving deeper than 3,000 meters (9,842 feet) and remaining submerged for over an hour. 7. Bump-head sunfish Wikimedia CommonsThe heaviest bony fish ever recorded was a bump-head sunfish found off Faial Island in the Azores on December 9, 2021. It weighed 2,744 kilograms (6,051 pounds), measured 3.25 meters (10.7 feet) long, and spanned 3.6 meters (11.8 feet) between its fin tips. Its flattened body and enormous fins make the sunfish appear almost unfinished. Yet this unusual design supports one of the ocean’s most distinctive giants.Water supports body mass more effectively than air, helping marine animals grow beyond the limits faced by land-dwelling creatures. Even so, the ocean continues to conceal its extremes. If the colossal squid could evade observation in its natural habitat for a century, other record-breaking animals may still be waiting in the depths.ConclusionWater supports immense bodies in a way that air cannot, allowing marine animals to grow far larger than most creatures on land. From the blue whale’s unmatched weight to the siphonophore’s extraordinary length, these ocean giants show that size can take remarkably different forms.Yet the most exciting possibility is that the list may not be complete. If the colossal squid remained unfilmed in its natural habitat for a century, other record-breaking creatures could still be moving through parts of the ocean humans have barely explored.

title: 93% of US nuclear reactor fuel foreign-sourced, core loads at 41M lbs
content: Commercial nuclear power plants in the United States loaded 40.9 million pounds of uranium into their reactor cores in 2025. This was a 15 percent drop from the 48.1 million pounds installed during 2024. “Uranium in fuel assemblies loaded into US civilian nuclear power reactors during 2025 contained 40.9 million pounds U3O8e, which is 15% less than the 48.1 million pounds loaded in 2024,” highlighted a report from the US Energy Information Administration.At the same time, power companies expanded their overall fuel reserves. Total commercial uranium stocks increased by 9 percent, reaching 170 million pounds by the end of 2025. These reserves contain material at various technical stages of the nuclear fuel cycle. They include raw uranium undergoing chemical conversion, material undergoing isotopic separation, and finished fuel rods ready for reactor cores. Reactor operators owned 118 million pounds of this total, which is a 3 percent increase over 2024 levels. “Uranium inventories owned by U.S. suppliers (converters, enrichers, fabricators, producers, brokers, and traders) totaled 51 million pounds U3O8e at the end of 2025, up 27% from 2024 year-end levels,” added the report.Over the next decade, American nuclear utilities will require a massive volume of fuel to maintain grid operations. Over the next 10 years, operators project a total baseline demand of 360 million pounds of uranium. Current long-term purchase agreements cover 174 million pounds of this requirement. The remaining 186 million pounds represent unfilled market demand that utilities must secure through new contracts.Preparing raw uranium for power generationPreparing raw uranium for power generation requires distinct chemical and technical processing steps. “In 2025, COOs delivered 32 million pounds U3O8e of natural uranium feed to U.S. and foreign enrichers,” remarked the report. Domestic enrichment plants processed 37 percent of this material. Foreign facilities handled the remaining 63 percent, which included major shipments of 5.5 million pounds to France and 2.4 million pounds to Russia.Isotopic enrichment is measured in separative work units. This metric measures the effort needed to separate fissile uranium-235 from non-fissile isotopes. US utilities purchased 13 million separative work units from four commercial sellers in 2025. “The average price paid by the COOs for the 13 million SWU was $108.70 per SWU in 2025, up 11% from the $97.66 per SWU paid in 2024,” noted the report.Foreign facilities provided 77 percent of these enrichment services. Russian enrichers supplied 26 percent of the total, followed by France at 18 percent, the United Kingdom at 14 percent, and the Netherlands at 8 percent. US enrichment facilities supplied the remaining 23 percent.Procurement volume declined but transaction costs increasedOverall uranium procurement declined in volume, but transaction costs increased. “The 2025 total of 46.9 million pounds U3O8e was 16% lower than the 2024 total of 55.9 million pounds U3O8e,” concluded the report.However, the weighted-average price rose 11 percent, moving from $52.71 per pound in 2024 to $58.46 per pound in 2025. Long-term contracts accounted for 87 percent of total deliveries at an average price of $55.91 per pound. Spot market purchases made up 13 percent of deliveries at a much higher average price of $76.01 per pound. Operators also signed 22 new purchase contracts during the year, securing 4 million pounds for 2025 delivery at an average cost of $70.46 per pound.Foreign mining operations supplied 93 percent of all uranium delivered to US reactors, while domestic production accounted for just 7 percent. Canadian facilities served as the leading supplier by providing 32 percent of all deliveries. Kazakhstan followed closely with 28 percent, while Australia supplied 15 percent. Uzbekistan provided 7 percent and Namibia supplied 4 percent. Specific delivery numbers for Russian-origin material were withheld by regulators to protect commercial confidentiality. Data from the Euratom Supply Agency shows that Canadian and Kazakh mining operations also remained the primary uranium suppliers for European power utilities throughout the same period.

title: California university gets access to $5B semiconductor R&D hub
content: AI chip development is pushing semiconductor engineers to rethink how quickly new technologies can move from research labs into production. New materials and manufacturing techniques can show promise in research settings, but scaling them for real chipmaking often takes years of testing. Applied Materials wants to cut some of that delay by putting university researchers closer to advanced manufacturing equipment.The company has named the University of California, Berkeley as a research collaborator at its new EPIC Center in Silicon Valley. Berkeley faculty and students will work alongside Applied engineers on semiconductor materials and process technologies tied to AI computing.Lab-to-fab gapA semiconductor breakthrough does not automatically translate into a production-ready technology. Researchers first need to prove that a new material or process works. Engineers then have to determine whether it can deliver consistent results across complex manufacturing conditions.That transition can create a major bottleneck. University laboratories may develop promising concepts without access to the same equipment used by commercial chip manufacturers.Applied’s EPIC Center is designed to bring those environments closer together. Berkeley researchers will gain access to industry-scale semiconductor equipment while working directly with Applied’s technical teams.The arrangement could let researchers identify manufacturing problems much earlier. It may also reduce the number of development cycles needed before a technology becomes ready for wider use.Berkeley’s chip legacyBerkeley enters the partnership with decades of semiconductor research behind it. The university established a research laboratory dedicated to integrated-circuit prototyping in 1962. Its researchers later produced breakthroughs that influenced the wider semiconductor industry.Those contributions include SPICE, a circuit simulation technology used to analyze electronic designs. Berkeley researchers also helped develop FinFET, a three-dimensional transistor architecture. FinFET eventually became a key part of advanced logic manufacturing. The technology now underpins generations of high-performance processors.That history makes Berkeley a natural research partner for a facility focused on accelerating semiconductor development. Mark Asta, dean of Berkeley’s College of Engineering, said EPIC could help move university inventions toward commercial products. The collaboration will also give students exposure to advanced industrial equipment.Shortening silicon cycleApplied Materials designed EPIC to tackle the long development timelines that often keep promising semiconductor technologies out of factories. Testing concepts with production-scale equipment can provide engineers with useful feedback much earlier. Researchers can see how materials and processes behave under conditions closer to commercial manufacturing.Applied says EPIC represents its largest US investment in advanced semiconductor equipment research and development. The Silicon Valley facility is on track to become operational in 2026. Berkeley and Applied already have research ties through shared laboratory facilities and semiconductor programs. Their connections include the Berkeley Emerging Technologies Research Center and CITRIS.The relationship also extends to talent. Berkeley alumni work at Applied Materials across engineering, research, and management positions. For the US semiconductor industry, that combination could matter as AI drives demand for increasingly advanced computing hardware. Moving research closer to manufacturing could help promising technologies make the jump from laboratory experiments to commercial chips faster.

title: Epirus' microwave weapon to counter drone swarms for US Marines
content: Drone swarms approaching US Marine Corps positions could soon face an invisible wall of electromagnetic energy. The country has awarded tech company Epirus an $11-million contract to deliver HAVOC, a vehicle-mounted high-power microwave system designed to disable multiple drones simultaneously.Derived from the company’s Leonidas weapon, the High-power Microwave Autonomous Vehicle Operational Capability will be integrated across manned and unmanned Marine Corps ground vehicles. The contract includes training, servicing and sustainment support, along with options for another system and related capabilities.Three times the powerHAVOC represents the next stage of the Expeditionary Directed Energy Counter-Swarm system, or ExDECS, delivered to the Marine Corps in 2025. While ExDECS introduced a deployable “one-to-many” approach for countering drones, its successor is expected to provide three times the power, greater range and improved ruggedness.The system uses solid-state high-power microwave weapon components and gallium nitride amplifiers to generate and strengthen electromagnetic energy.Instead of launching an interceptor at each target, it can produce electronic effects against multiple unmanned aerial systems within its coverage area.“This award highlights the Marine Corps’ commitment to fielding integrated, software-defined systems optimized for the complex and rapidly evolving drone threat,” Epirus CEO Andy Lowery said.“The HAVOC system will advance the one-to-many solution introduced with ExDECS and strengthen the Marines’ ability to deliver precise, low-collateral protection of high-value points and Marine warfighters,” he added. Its high-power microwave architecture is also designed to support continuous software-driven tuning. This could allow the weapon’s electronic effects to be adjusted as drone technologies and battlefield threats evolve.Microwave weapon goes mobileA universal sled mount will allow HAVOC to be installed on different Marine Corps ground vehicles instead of remaining tied to a single platform. That mobility could help units reposition the weapon with frontline forces or deploy it around vulnerable military infrastructure.HAVOC will also incorporate autonomous capabilities intended to reduce the decision-making burden on operators. This will be particularly important during swarm attacks, where personnel may need to detect, classify and engage numerous targets within seconds.The non-kinetic system can disable hostile drones without relying on conventional missiles or ammunition. Its low-collateral effects could make it useful around friendly troops, sensitive equipment and other locations where explosive interceptors pose additional risks.Protecting frontline assetsThe Marine Corps plans to use HAVOC alongside its existing low-altitude air-defense systems, including the FIM-92 Stinger, rather than as a replacement for them. The microwave weapon will become another layer within an architecture combining kinetic and non-kinetic defenses.Potential protection areas include refueling points, radars, communications equipment, power systems and other forward-deployed assets. HAVOC could also defend low-altitude air-defense units themselves, helping preserve systems responsible for countering larger aerial threats.The contract signals a broader attempt to move directed-energy counter-drone technology from demonstrations toward operationally relevant, production-ready systems. As inexpensive drones increasingly threaten expensive military equipment, HAVOC offers the Marines a way to engage multiple targets without firing one costly interceptor for every aircraft.

title: Floating vessel delivers power, water, and compute with zero emissions
content: Optimal Transit, a US-based firm, has designed a multi-purpose vessel capable of powering homes, producing clean water, and hosting AI compute workloads. Known as the Blue Economy VITAL 100 MW Kraaken, this zero-emission vessel generates enough fuel-free power for 32,000 homes, supplies fresh water to 150,000 people, and hosts 60 MW of AI compute capacity.The high-tech vessel uses a proven small waterplane area twin hull (SWATH) architecture paired with a flexible mooring system for offshore stability. It could provide an immediate utility alternative in areas mostly dependent on expensive diesel self-generation (e.g., Pacific Islands, sub-Saharan Africa, South/Southeast Asia).Three-in-one vessel Just five weeks after unveiling the Kraaken as an offshore, self-powered AI data center, the developers are shifting its payload. The new configuration redirects a massive fraction of its energy away from raw compute to export continuous electricity and fresh water directly to coastal grids. When first announced in July, the Kraaken made waves as a zero-emission floating data center powered by a patented Digital Ocean Thermal (DOT) engine.The VITAL 100 MW setup asks a different question: What if coastlines need utilities more than they need large language models? “The answer is a single vessel that can serve the equivalent of a small city – indefinitely, from offshore, with no connection to the existing grid,” said Jeff Kline, President of InMar Technologies.The updated layout turns the vessel into a tri-generation utility hub, continuously exporting 40 MW of clean electricity to power roughly 32,000 homes and producing 7.9 million gallons of fresh water daily for ~150,000 people via vacuum-flash desalination. And that’s not all. It retains 60 MW of onboard power dedicated to high-performance AI compute and sovereign data needs.Scalable “Power Parks”Power, fresh water, and data compute are all delivered to shore through a specialized quick-disconnect umbilical system. This setup allows the vessel to unplug and relocate within hours if threatened by severe weather or changing operational needs, then quickly reconnect once conditions clear.Interestingly, the new vessel also offers disaster relief by deploying within days to inject emergency power and fresh water directly into damaged coastal grids without depending on destroyed land infrastructure. Furthermore, the architecture could be scaled as per requirement. For instance, clustering five vessels into an offshore “Sovereign Power Park” would generate 200 MW of power, 40 million gallons of fresh water, and 300 MW of compute capacity. Altogether, it would be enough to support an entire metropolitan area without consuming land or fuel.The VITAL 100 MW integrates these features into a single offshore asset that requires no land, fuel, or grid connection. Building equivalent infrastructure on land would require three separate projects costing between $750 million and $1.33 billion. It also avoids six-to-ten-year delays due to permitting, zoning, and grid queue backlogs that the ready-to-operate vessel avoids completely.Hence, the system holds potential to cut land-based development costs by roughly 22 to 56 percent (costing 44 to 78 percent of traditional alternatives). Notably, the tech’s economic appeal is especially strong in developing and disaster-prone regions across sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and the Pacific, where unreliable grids force infrastructure to tap into diesel generators costing $0.40 to $0.55 per kilowatt-hour. In these markets, the vessel will be able to operate as a lucrative, stand-alone utility provider even without accounting for data center revenue.

title: Grok Bot is xAI's new 24/7 coworker that keeps working while you sleep
content: Elon Musk’s xAI wants Grok to do more than answer questions. Its new Grok Bot can take control of a computer and carry out digital work on its own, even after the user steps away.Each Bot gets a dedicated computer in the cloud, giving it a way to operate software directly. It can work inside the tools where the actual job needs to happen.That makes Grok Bot different from an AI assistant that simply produces text or suggests the next step. It is designed to execute multi-step jobs and return only when it needs human approval.The beta is available on desktop and iOS for SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Ultra, and Cursor Teams Premium subscribers. Enterprise users can join a waitlist for future access.Grok gets computer accessThe biggest technical difference sits beneath the chatbot interface. Grok Bot gains access to its own virtual computer and can interact with applications without requiring an API or MCP connection for every service.That could address a major limitation facing today’s AI agents. Many workplace tools were never designed for autonomous software to control them.Introducing Grok Bot, now in early beta.Bots are AI teammates that do real work for you. They sign in to your tools, use them just like you do, and come back with finished work. pic.twitter.com/uyfA97yo98— Grok Bot (@bot) August 11, 2026Grok Bot can instead work through existing interfaces much like a human operator. It can navigate websites, enter information, and continue through a task without waiting for another prompt.The computer-based approach also lets the Bot handle longer chains of work. Instead of stopping after generating a document, it can continue working inside the relevant application.That distinction matters when a task involves several actions that people normally perform manually. xAI says Grok Bot aims to complete those final steps instead of leaving users with an unfinished result.Bots can work togetherGrok Bot can also operate as part of a larger group of AI teammates. Multiple Bots can work on different parts of the same project while sharing context between them.A group chat can bring several Bots into one project, with one Bot coordinating work between the others. Bots can also pass assignments among themselves without requiring the user to manage every handoff.Grok Bot can learn workflows through demonstrations as well. A person can show a Bot how a task works, after which the system can save that process as a reusable routine.Later corrections can influence how the Bot handles similar work. That could reduce the need to repeatedly explain the same process.Grok Bot remembersMemory gives Grok Bot another layer of autonomy. It can retain information from previous conversations and corrections when returning to unfinished work.The Bot can also follow up when a conversation stalls or an assigned task remains incomplete. xAI says it can become more proactive over time and recognize when human approval is necessary.That changes the user’s role from constant operator to supervisor. Instead of repeatedly prompting an AI model, someone can delegate a job and wait for the system to return with the result.For US businesses, the computer-use approach could prove useful because many companies rely on software without dedicated AI integrations. An agent that can operate those interfaces directly would not need every vendor to build a new connection first.Grok Bot remains in beta, so its reliability across complicated workflows will need broader testing. Giving an AI agent its own computer nevertheless pushes Musk’s favorite Grok toward a model where AI can perform digital work instead of simply explaining how people should do it.

title: Huge space radars to track tiny objects could be assembled by robots
content: Space is becoming increasingly crowded, and tracking the objects orbiting Earth is becoming a harder engineering problem. NASA is now funding a particularly unconventional idea that could eventually help build enormous radar antennas in space using robots and modular metamaterials.The concept, led by Duke University electrical and computer engineering professor David Smith, was selected for a 2026 NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) Phase I study. The project is called Robotically Assembled Electromagnetic Metamaterials for Long-Range Space Situational Awareness. This is still a research concept and not an operational space radar. The Phase I work is intended to determine whether the underlying approach could eventually become practical.Why build a radar in space?Space surveillance networks already use powerful ground-based radars to track objects in orbit. NASA says systems such as the upgraded Space Fence can track objects down to roughly four inches (about 10 cm) in low Earth orbit. But tracking smaller objects, or monitoring spacecraft at much greater distances, becomes considerably more difficult.The basic physics creates the problem. The farther away a target is, the larger the radar’s effective aperture needs to be for a given detection performance. For objects beyond low Earth orbit, NASA says the size requirements of ground-based arrays can become impractical.Putting the radar closer to the objects could help. But conventional space antennas have an obvious limitation. They have to survive launch and fit inside a rocket’s available volume. That is where the unusual part begins.What if the antenna was built after launch?Instead of launching one enormous antenna, Smith’s concept would send its components into space and have robots assemble them there. NASA already has relevant technology under development through ARMADAS, or Automated Reconfigurable Mission Adaptive Digital Assembly Systems. The project uses relatively simple robots to assemble standardized structural building blocks called voxels.In a NASA demonstration, three robots autonomously assembled hundreds of these blocks into a structure roughly the size of a shed. The robots operated in an inchworm-like fashion, transporting, positioning, and fastening the modules. The idea is therefore less like sending a giant antenna into orbit and more like sending a construction kit.Where metamaterials enter the pictureThe building blocks would not simply be pieces of metal. Smith specializes in electromagnetic metamaterials. These are artificially structured materials whose geometry can be engineered to interact with electromagnetic waves in unusual ways. His Duke group famously demonstrated a microwave-frequency metamaterial “invisibility cloak” in 2006, showing that engineered structures could manipulate electromagnetic waves in ways conventional materials could not easily achieve.For the NASA concept, metamaterials could effectively become the building blocks of a huge electromagnetic aperture. Rather than treating the antenna as one enormous conventional structure, researchers could assemble many small electromagnetic elements into a much larger system. NASA says the project will investigate metamaterial designs using numerical modeling, while incorporating the practical constraints of robotic assembly demonstrated by ARMADAS.Why make it enormous?For radar and other electromagnetic sensing systems, a larger aperture can provide advantages in resolution and sensitivity. NASA notes that increasing aperture size can improve the performance of beam-steering, radar, and observation missions.That could potentially make an assembled-in-space system useful for tracking increasingly distant or difficult-to-detect objects. And the concept isn’t necessarily limited to debris tracking. NASA says the same design principles could eventually apply to large-aperture instruments used for Earth observation and deep-space communications.The hard part is making it surviveThe concept also comes with major unanswered questions. A huge structure assembled from thousands or millions of modules would have to remain mechanically and electrically reliable in orbit. Individual components could be damaged by micrometeoroids or orbital debris, while the structure would have to tolerate thermal cycling and the harsh space environment.An especially challenging aspect is that the radar would have to operate in the same debris-filled environment it is designed to monitor. A large modular structure could potentially be struck by the same kind of high-speed debris it is intended to track, raising questions about how individual damaged metamaterial elements would be replaced and whether a localized failure could affect the wider antenna. These are not limitations NASA identifies in its Phase I description, but they illustrate the practical questions that would have to be answered if the concept progresses beyond the study stage. NASA’s ARMADAS work is already exploring autonomous construction and reconfiguration, but its demonstrated structures are laboratory-scale compared with the giant apertures envisioned for advanced space sensing.That is precisely why the new project is interesting. It combines three technologies that have largely developed separately. Metamaterials, autonomous robotic construction, and large space structures. If the concept works, the biggest breakthrough may not simply be a better radar. It could be a new way of building enormous infrastructure in orbit without having to launch that infrastructure as a single enormous machine.

title: Intel silicon quantum chip points to hidden atomic disorder that disrupts qubits
content: Scientists in the US have found a hidden atomic disorder inside silicon quantum devices that could help answer the long-standing question of why some qubits fail or perform inconsistently.The project was carried out by a team at Argonne National Laboratory (ANL). The researchers studied an industrially manufactured 12-qubit-class silicon quantum dot processor from Intel. For the study, they used highly sensitive measurements to map variations in the material at the nanoscale. Their analysis traced the long-standing qubit problem to random changes at the atomic level.The findings could lead to the development of more reliable silicon qubits and larger quantum computers. Silicon spin qubits are promising because they can use existing semiconductor manufacturing methods. “This study revealed that disorder on the atomic scale in the quantum well is the main source of variability of valley splitting,” ANL said. Tracing qubit failuresUnlike conventional computer bits, which represent information as either 0 or 1, silicon spin qubits rely on the spin of individual electrons. An electron’s spin can point up or down in a magnetic field, somewhat like a tiny compass needle.To create these qubits, scientists trap a single electron inside an extremely thin layer of silicon known as a quantum well. Electrons in silicon also have another quantum property known as a valley state. The energy difference between these states is called valley splitting.The Chicago quantum computing testbed at Argonne National Laboratory (ANL).Credit: Argonne National Laboratory (ANL)Valley splitting competes with the electron spin states used to perform quantum computations. Once the splitting becomes too small, the electrons can leak into unwanted valley states. This can lead to errors and reduce the fidelity of the qubit.That said, valley splitting can vary greatly between devices. Even though the team suspected that material defects and inconsistencies played a role, the underlying cause of these variations remained unclear. To investigate the issue the research team used the Chicago Quantum Computing Testbed, which is operated by the Q-NEXT National Quantum Information Science Research Center. The facility is the first full-stack, solid-state qubit testbed at a US National Laboratory.Testing silicon qubitsThe scientists relied on electrical spectroscopy to measure valley splitting while moving the position of a quantum dot along the silicon quantum well. This made it possible to create a nanoscale map showing how valley splitting changed from one location to another.They then evaluated how these variations changed across different distances and found that random atomic changes in the alloyed quantum well were the main cause of valley splitting variability.Knowing where the variability originates could help semiconductor manufacturers to focus on improving the materials and fabrication processes for silicon quantum device production. The collaboration linked Intel’s semiconductor manufacturing with ANL’s quantum expertise.According to Jonathan Marcks, PhD, a scientist at ANL, the work could speed up research by removing one of the field’s biggest hurdles. “It can be difficult to build even a few quantum dot qubits,” he said in a press statement. “But with Intel, the prospect of making a ton of qubits on a practical device using quantum dots suddenly seems a lot more realistic.”Reducing the atomic variations could help manufacturers produce silicon qubits with more consistent valley splitting and higher fidelity. This could make it easier to scale quantum processors to much larger numbers of qubits. The research was funded by the US Department of Energy’s Office of Science through the Q-NEXT center.The study has been published in the journal Nature Communications.

title: JCB’s 1,600-hp hydrogen car hits 406 mph in world speed record attempt
content: JCB’s hydrogen-powered Hydromax streamliner has reached 406.320 mph (653.2 km/h) at Utah’s Bonneville Salt Flats, setting a provisional world land speed record for a hydrogen internal combustion vehicle. The run took place on August 11, with Wing Commander Andy Green OBE behind the wheel. The record still needs formal ratification by the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA).The 32-foot British-built car made two runs in opposite directions within one hour, following FIA requirements for a flying kilometer record. It recorded 400.623 mph on the first pass and 412.135 mph on the return. Those figures produced a two-way average of 406.320 mph.A new benchmark for hydrogen combustionHydromax’s result more than doubles the previous FIA-recognized hydrogen internal combustion record. That mark was 185.5 mph, set by BMW’s H2R in 2004.The attempt falls into FIA Category A, Group XIV, Class 7 World Flying Record Start Land Speed Record. Final certification is still pending, so the 406.320 mph figure remains provisional.The car also moved beyond several major hydrogen and diesel milestones. It surpassed JCB Dieselmax’s 350.092 mph diesel record from 2006, which Green also drove at Bonneville. JCB said Hydromax produces no CO₂ at the tailpipe. Its speed also exceeded the 303 mph record previously achieved by a hydrogen fuel cell vehicle.Two production-based engines deliver 1,600 hpJCB built Hydromax around two hydrogen-fueled internal combustion engines derived from its production “digger” engines. Together, they produce 1,600 horsepower. The engines are manufactured at JCB’s facility in Foston, Derbyshire, England.The company says the power units are fundamentally the same hydrogen combustion engines being developed for its construction equipment. The program forms part of JCB’s £100 million hydrogen development effort.The approach gives the streamliner a direct connection to technology intended for working machines. Rather than using fuel cells to convert hydrogen into electricity, Hydromax burns hydrogen inside modified combustion engines.Green returns to BonnevilleJCB Chairman Anthony Bamford said the attempt builds on the company’s Dieselmax achievement at Bonneville two decades ago.“Twenty years ago we came to Bonneville with JCB Dieselmax and showed what British engineering could do with diesel power. Today we have done it again—this time with engines powered by hydrogen,” Bamford said.Green, who holds the outright land speed record at 763.035 mph and is the only person to break the sound barrier on land, described the project as a privilege.“Bonneville is the spiritual home of the world land speed record, and JCB Hydromax has just written itself into that history,” he said, calling the streamliner “stable, strong and fast” while praising “a world-class team and superb technology.”Speed test set the stageHydromax had already shown its pace during a warmup appearance at the Southern California Timing Association’s Bonneville Speed Week. It recorded a 368.347 mph average in the Blown Gas Streamliner AA/BGS 500-plus cubic inch class, setting a new SCTA mark before the latest record attempt.

title: Just 1% strain unlocks hidden magnetism for future electronic devices
content: Rice University researchers have found a way to isolate a single magnetic domain in manganese telluride, giving them a clearer view of its magnetic structure and a new way to control an electrical effect in the material.The work focuses on altermagnetism, a recently recognized form of magnetism that could offer a different route to spin-based electronics. Researchers are interested in altermagnets because they may combine useful properties of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets while potentially enabling faster, lower-heat information processing.The challenge is that manganese telluride normally forms multiple magnetic domains, which can point in different directions. Their signals can overlap, making it difficult to determine the material’s intrinsic magnetic structure.The Rice team addressed the problem by applying uniaxial strain, stretching the manganese telluride in one direction. This forced the material into a single-domain state that could be measured more clearly.Stretching reveals hidden magnetism“Altermagnets like hexagonal manganese telluride typically form multidomain structures where the magnetic forces divide into separate equivalent domains that spin in different directions to satisfy the underlying threefold rotational symmetry of the hexagonal lattice,” said Dai, the Sam and Helen Worden Professor of Physics and Astronomy. “The signals from these coexisting domains could overlap, making it hard to know what the underlying magnetic structure actually is. Here, we were able to apply a uniaxial strain, which resulted in a single magnetic domain we could clearly resolve into the underlying magnetic structure.”The single-domain state also allowed the researchers to observe a sharp feature in the material’s anomalous Hall effect, which produces a voltage across a material when electrical current flows through it and is influenced by its magnetic properties.At about 230 kelvin, or minus 45 degrees Fahrenheit, the researchers found that strain could change the polarity of this Hall signal. The electrical response could therefore be switched without substantially changing the material’s underlying magnetic interactions.“By applying the uniaxial strain, we were able to finally resolve the magnetic structure of manganese telluride,” said Sijie Xu, a Rice graduate student and co-first author. “This also allowed us to see a remarkably sharp feature in the anomalous Hall signal, which describes a lateral voltage generated when an electrical current flows through the material due to its magnetic structure.”Strain offers temperature alternativeThe researchers believe the tunability comes from changes in the material’s Berry curvature, a property that describes how electrons behave as they move through a material’s electronic structure.The scale of the required strain is also significant. The team’s calculations suggest that a 1% change in strain could produce an effect equivalent to changing the temperature by about 150 kelvin.Temperature is commonly used to tune magnetic properties, but that approach is difficult to apply in practical electronics. Mechanical strain could provide another control mechanism if it can eventually be incorporated into devices.“Essentially, we can use this uniaxial strain to tune the anomalous Hall effect, switching it from one charge to another,” said Zhaoyu Liu, co-first author and researcher in Dai’s group. “Because the magnetic interactions remain largely unchanged, the effect likely originates from strain-induced changes in the Berry curvature.”The researchers see the result as an early step toward using altermagnets in spin-transport technologies, including future memory and high-frequency electronics.“This work brings us one step closer to controlling altermagnets for next-generation spin-transport applications,” Dai said.The study was published in Physical Review X.

title: NVIDIA launches Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for 4x faster agent tasks
content: NVIDIA has launched a smaller open model designed to handle the repetitive, high-volume tasks that keep autonomous agents running, aiming to cut the cost and latency of long-running agent workloads.Called Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, the model has 30 billion total parameters but activates only 3 billion for each token. NVIDIA says this mixture-of-experts design allows it to deliver the capacity of a larger model while using compute closer to that of a much smaller one.The model is aimed at the execution layer of autonomous agents, where systems repeatedly call tools, check results, run commands, and delegate tasks. Instead of using a large reasoning model for every step, developers can use Lightning for routine work while reserving larger models for planning and complex decisions.Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is also designed to run locally, including on NVIDIA’s DGX Spark, Jetson systems and GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards. It can also be deployed in data centers, giving developers options for running high-volume workloads closer to where they are generated.Smaller models take overNVIDIA is positioning Lightning as part of a broader shift toward systems that use multiple models rather than relying on one model for every task. Larger reasoning models can handle planning and orchestration, while smaller models take care of execution.The model has been trained with popular agent harnesses in mind, including OpenClaw and Hermes Agent. NVIDIA says this training helps agents make more accurate tool calls while reducing latency during repetitive tasks.The company is also releasing the model as an open offering, including its weights, training data, and recipes under the OpenMDW-1.1 license. Developers can fine-tune it using NVIDIA’s NeMo tools or run reinforcement learning and environment-based evaluations.NVIDIA says Nemotron 3.5 Lightning can deliver up to four times the output speed of similar-sized models. On PinchBench, it reached 86 percent accuracy while completing 10,000 tasks 30% faster than Qwen3.6 35B at similar accuracy.The model also supports speculative decoding, a technique that allows multiple tokens to be proposed and then efficiently checked. NVIDIA has included multi-token prediction during training and provides two additional draft models, DSpark and DFlash, for different inference workloads.Routing work by complexityThe launch also highlights NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard, a model-routing library designed to direct different tasks to different models. A complex request can be sent to a more capable reasoning model, while routine execution can be routed to Nemotron 3.5 Lightning.That approach could reduce the amount of expensive compute used by always-on agents, particularly systems that perform thousands of small actions over long periods.The model is supported across a growing ecosystem of inference platforms, agent frameworks and cloud services, including Ollama, LM Studio, Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.NVIDIA says Nemotron 3.5 Lightning can be downloaded through Hugging Face and ModelScope, while developers can also access it through NVIDIA’s own platform and OpenRouter.

title: New $472M electronic brain modernizes aging CH-47 Chinook helicopters
content: The U.S. Army is putting up to $472 million behind a new push to keep its CH-47 Chinook helicopters ready for future missions. Collins Aerospace will provide engineering support focused on modernizing the aircraft’s avionics and keeping aging systems in service.The effort goes beyond replacing older electronics. Collins will help create a more adaptable avionics setup, allowing the Army to introduce new capabilities without repeatedly reworking the aircraft’s core systems.That matters for the CH-47, which remains a key heavy-lift helicopter for the U.S. military. Its long service life also means engineers must balance new technology with equipment designed years or decades earlier.Easier upgradesAvionics sit at the center of how modern military aircraft communicate, navigate, and manage mission systems. As those technologies advance, older components can become difficult or expensive to maintain.Collins will support the Army in tackling those obsolescence issues across the Chinook fleet. Engineers will also work on integrating new capabilities more efficiently as operational requirements change.The approach could make future upgrades less disruptive. Instead of treating each new capability as a major integration exercise, the Army can work from a more flexible electronic foundation.“Collins equips the Chinook with advanced avionics that integrate communication, navigation and mission subsystems,” said Jenny Miller, vice president and general manager of Vision and Sensing Systems at Collins Aerospace.Miller said the company’s long-running work with the Army helps the fleet evolve as its requirements change.Open architectureA major part of the effort involves open and reusable avionics architecture. That design philosophy can give military engineers more freedom when introducing new hardware and software.It also has implications beyond the CH-47. The Army wants greater commonality across its aviation fleet, making it easier to apply proven avionics approaches across multiple aircraft.For the Chinook, common architecture could reduce the engineering effort involved in future technology insertions. It can also help limit integration costs and shorten the time needed to bring upgrades into service.The strategy addresses a persistent problem for military aviation. Aircraft often remain operational long after the technology inside them has become outdated.Keeping the platform viable therefore requires more than maintaining existing components. Engineers need an architecture that can absorb new technology without forcing extensive changes throughout the aircraft.Keeping Chinooks readyThe new engineering work gives the Army a way to address both sides of that challenge. Collins can support current avionics sustainment while preparing the CH-47 for future upgrades.The contract has a maximum value of $472 million, giving the Army access to engineering support as modernization requirements evolve. That flexibility could prove important as the Army introduces new mission equipment and updates cockpit systems over the Chinook’s service life.For the Chinook fleet, the larger goal is straightforward. The Army wants its helicopters to remain operationally relevant without making every new avionics upgrade a major redesign effort.A more reusable architecture could help engineers get there while improving commonality across the Army’s broader aviation fleet.
